title: Web3 Security: Complete Protection Guide
subtitle: Learn to protect yourself and find vulnerabilities in the blockchain ecosystem

intro.title: Understanding Web3 Security
intro.content:
Web3 security is fundamentally different from traditional cybersecurity. In the blockchain world, code is law - once a transaction is executed, it cannot be reversed. A single approval to a malicious contract can drain your entire wallet in seconds.

Since 2020, over $10 billion has been lost to hacks, exploits, and scams in the DeFi ecosystem. Understanding security isn't optional - it's essential for survival in this space.

This guide will take you from basic personal protection to understanding complex protocol vulnerabilities, and even show you how to earn by finding bugs.

threat_landscape.title: The Threat Landscape
threat_landscape.content: Before protecting yourself, you need to understand what you're up against. Web3 threats range from simple phishing attacks to sophisticated smart contract exploits.

common_attacks.title: Common Attack Types
common_attacks.content:
1. Phishing & Social Engineering
Fake websites, Discord DMs, and impersonator accounts remain the #1 way users lose funds. Attackers create pixel-perfect copies of popular dApps or pose as support staff.

2. Approval Exploits
When you approve a token for spending, you're giving that contract permission to move your tokens. Unlimited approvals (common default) mean a compromised contract can drain everything.

3. Smart Contract Vulnerabilities
Bugs in code like reentrancy, integer overflow, or access control issues that allow attackers to steal funds from protocols.

4. Flash Loan Attacks
Sophisticated attacks that borrow millions in uncollateralized loans to manipulate prices and drain protocols, all within a single transaction.

attack_vectors.title: Attack Vectors
attack_vectors.content:
Frontend Attacks: DNS hijacking, CDN compromises, or malicious browser extensions can replace legitimate transactions with malicious ones.

Private Key Theft: Malware, compromised hardware, or poor operational security can expose private keys directly.

Oracle Manipulation: Manipulating price feeds that DeFi protocols rely on for liquidations and swaps.

Bridge Exploits: Cross-chain bridges are high-value targets due to the large amount of locked assets.

personal_security.title: Personal Security Essentials
personal_security.content: Your first line of defense is your own security practices. Most losses come from preventable user-side mistakes.

wallet_safety.title: Wallet Safety
wallet_safety.content:
Hardware Wallets: Use hardware wallets (Ledger, Trezor) for any significant holdings. They keep your private keys offline and require physical confirmation for transactions.

Wallet Segregation: Use separate wallets for different purposes:

  • Hot wallet: Small amounts for daily use and minting
  • Cold wallet: Main holdings, never connected to random dApps
  • Burner wallet: For testing new protocols or risky interactions

Transaction Previews: Modern wallets like Rabby show transaction simulations before signing. Always review what you're actually approving.

approval_management.title: Managing Token Approvals
approval_management.content:
Every time you interact with a DeFi protocol, you likely grant token approvals. These permissions persist forever unless revoked.

Best Practices:

  • Regularly audit approvals using Revoke.cash or De.Fi
  • Set specific amounts instead of unlimited approvals when possible
  • Revoke approvals for protocols you no longer use
  • Be suspicious of requests for unusual token approvals

Example: The BadgerDAO exploit ($120M lost) exploited malicious approvals injected via a compromised frontend. Users who had granted unlimited approvals lost their entire positions.

phishing_protection.title: Phishing Protection
phishing_protection.content:
URL Verification: Always verify you're on the correct domain. Bookmark official sites. Be especially careful with:

  • Google ad results (often used for phishing)
  • Links from Discord/Twitter DMs
  • QR codes from unknown sources

Transaction Simulation: Use tools like Pocket Universe or Blowfish that simulate transactions before signing. They'll warn you if a transaction would drain your wallet.

Browser Extensions: Install ScamSniffer or Wallet Guard to get real-time warnings about known phishing sites.

contract_security.title: Smart Contract Security
contract_security.content: Understanding smart contract security helps you evaluate protocols and, if you're a developer, write safer code.

common_vulnerabilities.title: Common Vulnerabilities
common_vulnerabilities.content:
Reentrancy: When a contract makes an external call before updating its state, allowing attackers to re-enter and drain funds repeatedly. The DAO hack ($60M) was a reentrancy attack.

Access Control: Missing or improper permission checks that allow unauthorized users to call privileged functions.

Integer Overflow/Underflow: Mathematical operations that wrap around, potentially allowing attackers to create tokens from nothing or bypass balance checks.

Oracle Manipulation: Using spot prices or easily manipulable price sources that can be exploited with flash loans.

Tools for Detection: Static analyzers like Slither can automatically detect many common vulnerabilities. MythX provides symbolic execution for deeper analysis.

audit_process.title: Understanding Audits
audit_process.content:
What Audits Cover:

  • Code review for logical errors and vulnerabilities
  • Economic attack analysis
  • Gas optimization recommendations
  • Best practices compliance

Audit Limitations:

  • Audits are a snapshot in time - changes after audit may introduce bugs
  • Auditors can miss issues - even audited protocols get hacked
  • Not all auditors are equal - check the firm's track record

Evaluating Audits: Check CertiK's security leaderboard, read the actual audit reports (not just "audited by"), and look for multiple audits from reputable firms.

formal_verification.title: Formal Verification
formal_verification.content:
Formal verification uses mathematical proofs to verify code behaves as intended. It's the highest level of security assurance but also the most expensive and time-consuming.

When It's Used:

  • Core DeFi primitives (Uniswap V2, Compound)
  • Bridge contracts holding billions
  • Token contracts with high TVL

For most users, checking if a protocol has formal verification is a strong positive signal, but its absence isn't necessarily a red flag for smaller protocols.

case_studies.title: Learning from Real Hacks
case_studies.content: The best way to understand security is to study real attacks. Each major hack teaches valuable lessons about what can go wrong.

reentrancy.title: The DAO Hack (2016)
reentrancy.content: The attack that changed Ethereum forever and led to the creation of Ethereum Classic.

case_dao.title: The Original Reentrancy Attack
case_dao.description: The DAO held ~15% of all ETH at the time. The attacker exploited a reentrancy vulnerability in the withdrawal function, recursively calling it before the balance was updated. This allowed them to drain 3.6 million ETH (~$60M at the time). The attack was so significant that the Ethereum community hard-forked to recover the funds, creating Ethereum Classic as the original chain.

flash_loan_attacks.title: Flash Loan Attacks
flash_loan_attacks.content: Flash loans enable attacks previously impossible - borrowing millions with no collateral to manipulate prices within a single transaction.

case_euler.title: Euler Finance Hack - $197M
case_euler.description: In March 2023, an attacker exploited a vulnerability in Euler's donation function combined with a flaw in the liquidation logic. Using a flash loan from Aave, they manipulated the protocol's accounting to create a situation where they could liquidate themselves at a profit. The attack drained $197M, making it one of the largest DeFi hacks ever. Remarkably, the attacker eventually returned most of the funds after negotiations.

bridge_hacks.title: Bridge Vulnerabilities
bridge_hacks.content: Cross-chain bridges are honeypots holding billions in locked assets. Their complex validator/signature schemes have been repeatedly exploited.

case_ronin.title: Ronin Bridge Hack - $625M
case_ronin.description: The Axie Infinity Ronin bridge required 5 of 9 validators to sign withdrawals. The North Korean Lazarus Group compromised 5 validators through social engineering (fake job offer) and a third-party validator. They drained 173,600 ETH and $25.5M USDC. The attack went undetected for 6 days until a user tried to withdraw. This highlighted the risks of centralized bridge security and poor monitoring.

earning.title: Earning Through Security
earning.content: Web3 security is one of the most lucrative fields in blockchain. Top security researchers earn millions through bug bounties and audit contests.

bug_bounties.title: Bug Bounty Hunting
bug_bounties.content:
Immunefi is the largest Web3 bug bounty platform with over $150M in bounties paid. Top payouts include:

  • Wormhole: $10M for a critical vulnerability
  • Aurora: $6M bounty paid
  • Polygon: $2M for a consensus bug

Getting Started:

  1. Learn Solidity and common vulnerability patterns
  2. Study past exploits and audit reports
  3. Start with smaller protocols to build experience
  4. Document your findings clearly for maximum payout

audit_contests.title: Audit Contests
audit_contests.content:
Competitive auditing platforms let you compete with other auditors to find bugs:

Code4rena: Community-driven audit contests with prize pools up to $1M. Results are public, building your reputation.

Sherlock: Combines auditing with insurance coverage. Auditors stake tokens backing their work.

CodeHawks (Cyfrin): Educational focus with structured learning paths alongside contests.

Tips for Success:

  • Focus on understanding the protocol's business logic first
  • Look for edge cases and invariants that can be broken
  • Write clear, reproducible proof-of-concepts
  • Collaborate and learn from top auditors' reports

security_career.title: Building a Security Career
security_career.content:
Career Paths:

  • Independent Auditor: Freelance, high earning potential, flexible schedule
  • Audit Firm: Structured environment, steady work, learn from peers
  • Protocol Security: In-house security at major protocols
  • Security Tooling: Building detection and monitoring tools

Skill Development:

  • Master Solidity and EVM internals
  • Learn fuzzing and formal verification basics
  • Study economics and mechanism design
  • Build a public track record through contests

tools_deep_dive.title: Security Tools Deep Dive
tools_deep_dive.content: The right tools can dramatically improve your security posture, whether you're a user, developer, or auditor.

static_analysis.title: Static Analysis Tools
static_analysis.content:
Slither (Trail of Bits): The most widely used Solidity static analyzer. Detects common vulnerabilities, optimizations, and code quality issues. Free and open source.

MythX: Commercial tool using symbolic execution and SMT solvers for deeper analysis. Can find bugs that static analysis misses.

Aderyn: Newer tool focused on speed and integration with modern development workflows.

Usage: Run static analysis on every commit. Integrate into CI/CD pipelines. Don't ignore warnings - investigate each one.

monitoring.title: Real-Time Monitoring
monitoring.content:
Forta: Decentralized detection network with community-built bots monitoring for threats. Covers exploit detection, governance attacks, and unusual activity.

OpenZeppelin Defender: Operations platform for secure contract management. Includes automated transaction execution, upgrades, and monitoring.

What to Monitor:

  • Large value transfers
  • Unusual function calls
  • Governance proposals
  • Oracle price deviations
  • Approval changes

transaction_analysis.title: Transaction Analysis
transaction_analysis.content:
When something goes wrong, you need to understand what happened:

Phalcon (BlockSec): Transaction explorer with call tracing, fund flow analysis, and exploit detection. Essential for post-mortem analysis.

Tx Tracer (OpenChain): Free transaction tracer with calldata decoding. Great for understanding complex transactions.

Tenderly: Transaction simulation and debugging platform. Use it to test transactions before sending or debug failed ones.

reentrancy.definition: A vulnerability where a contract makes an external call before updating its state, allowing the called contract to call back and repeat the action before the first call completes.

approval.definition: Permission granted to a smart contract to spend tokens on your behalf. Unlimited approvals allow spending any amount of that token forever unless revoked.

front_running.definition: When someone observes a pending transaction and submits their own transaction with higher gas to execute before it, profiting from the price movement the original transaction would cause.

oracle_manipulation.definition: Artificially moving the price reported by an oracle (price feed) to exploit protocols that rely on that price for liquidations, swaps, or lending.

private_key.definition: The secret cryptographic key that controls access to a blockchain address. Anyone with the private key has full control over the associated funds.

phishing.definition: Fraudulent attempts to steal credentials or trick users into signing malicious transactions, typically through fake websites or impersonation.

bug_bounty.definition: A reward program where protocols pay security researchers for responsibly disclosing vulnerabilities before they can be exploited.

formal_verification.definition: Using mathematical proofs to verify that code behaves exactly as specified, providing the highest level of assurance that no bugs exist in the verified properties.

honeypot.definition: A malicious token or contract designed to let you buy in but prevent you from selling, trapping your funds permanently.

rugpull.definition: When developers abandon a project after extracting user funds, typically by draining liquidity pools or exploiting admin functions.
